title: Cut the text into units to point at
statement: Cut each text into units a question can point at, a spoken line with its speaker, a verse line or a sentence, and never count stage directions as evidence.
detail: The lesson engine parses every text into numbered units its blocks point at, a verse line with its speaker in a play, a line in a poem and a sentence in prose, and keeps stage directions for display but never as evidence (`g9/transformer/src/text.js`, lines 1-2). Line numbers from the writer are mapped to spoken lines only (`g9/transformer/src/mechanics/util.js`, line 28). The preferred quotation matcher, a 3D version's own, refuses a quotation that runs across a stage direction or across two speeches (`g9/transformer/src/glue/threejs.js`, lines 53-54). The code gives no reason for the drama rules.
against: Without the 3D version's tools, the fallback matcher joins consecutive spoken lines with the directions left out, so a quotation can then run across a direction or two speeches: "Find a quotation in the text. It may span consecutive lines." (`g9/transformer/src/text.js`, line 52). A later run found: Where a lesson teaches play conventions, a stage direction is the evidence: an archived Grade 3 drama lesson requires an item that only a stage direction, not a spoken line, answers. The rule never to count stage directions as evidence holds only where they are not what is taught (`incept-package-hub/course-packages/archive/g3-reading-v2/authoring/prompts/u02.md`).

evidence.quote: A text becomes numbered units that mechanics can point at: a verse line with its speaker (drama), a line (poem), … or a sentence (prose). Stage directions are kept for display but are never evidence.
Writer line numbers (L numbers) -> unit indices, keeping only spoken lines.
punctuation, case and apostrophes aside, never across a … stage direction or two speeches.
